notes.summary: Moments describe the shape of a distribution. The first moment gives the centre, the second the spread, the third the lack of symmetry (skewness) and the fourth the peakedness (kurtosis). Paper 2 asks 6 to 10 questions: converting raw moments to central moments, Karl Pearson's and Bowley's coefficients of skewness, β₁, β₂, γ₁, γ₂, and reading the shape from mean, median and mode.

concepts.title: Raw and central moments
concepts.body:
• Raw moment about a point A: μ′r = Σf(x − A)r ÷ N. About zero (A = 0) they are called moments about the origin.
  • Central moment (about the mean): μr = Σf(x − x̄)r ÷ N.
  • μ0 = 1, μ1 = 0 always, μ2 = variance.
  • μ′1 about A = x̄ − A, so mean = A + μ′1.

concepts.title: Converting raw moments to central moments
concepts.body:
Write μ′1, μ′2, μ′3, μ′4 for the moments about any point A.

  • μ2 = μ′2 − μ′1²
  • μ3 = μ′3 − 3μ′2μ′1 + 2μ′1³
  • μ4 = μ′4 − 4μ′3μ′1 + 6μ′2μ′1² − 3μ′1⁴

These come from expanding (x − A − μ′1)r with binomial coefficients. The last two terms join: in μ3, +3 − 1 = +2; in μ4, −4 + 1 = −3.

Mini example: about A = 4, μ′1 = 1, μ′2 = 10, μ′3 = 30, μ′4 = 100. Mean = 5. μ2 = 10 − 1 = 9. μ3 = 30 − 30 + 2 = 2. μ4 = 100 − 120 + 60 − 3 = 37.

Change of origin and scale: central moments do not change when a constant is added. If u = (x − A) ÷ h, then μr(x) = hr μr(u).

Sheppard's correction for grouped data with width h: corrected μ2 = μ2 − h²/12; μ3 needs no correction; corrected μ4 = μ4 − (h²/2)μ2 + (7/240)h⁴.

concepts.title: Skewness: what it means
concepts.body:
Skewness is lack of symmetry. In a symmetric curve the two tails are mirror images.

ShapeLong tailOrder of averagesSign of μ3
SymmetricNoneMean = Median = Mode0
Positively skewedRightMean > Median > ModePositive
Negatively skewedLeftMean < Median < ModeNegative
  • In positive skewness Q3 − Median > Median − Q1.
  • Income distributions are usually positively skewed (a few very high incomes). Age at death in rich countries is negatively skewed.
  • Skewness tells the direction of the tail; dispersion tells the amount of spread. They are different ideas.

concepts.title: Measures of skewness
concepts.body:
MeasureFormulaUsual range
Karl Pearson (first)Skp = (Mean − Mode) ÷ σUsually −1 to +1
Karl Pearson (second)Skp = 3(Mean − Median) ÷ σ−3 to +3
Bowley (quartile)SkB = (Q3 + Q1 − 2Md) ÷ (Q3 − Q1)−1 to +1
Kelly (percentile)(P90 + P10 − 2P50) ÷ (P90 − P10)−1 to +1
Momentβ1 = μ3² ÷ μ2³, γ1 = ±√β1 (sign of μ3) = μ3 ÷ σ³β1 ≥ 0

Bowley's measure uses only the middle 50% of data, so it suits open-end classes. β1 is always non-negative, so it cannot show direction; γ1 takes the sign of μ3.

concepts.title: Kurtosis
concepts.body:
Kurtosis measures how peaked (or heavy-tailed) a curve is compared with the normal curve.

  • β2 = μ4 ÷ μ2², γ2 = β2 − 3 (excess kurtosis).
Typeβ2γ2Shape
Leptokurtic> 3> 0More peaked, heavier tails
Mesokurtic= 3= 0Normal curve
Platykurtic< 3< 0Flatter top

Memory hook: lepto = "leaps" up, platy = flat like a plate. Always β2 ≥ 1 and β2 ≥ β1 + 1.

Mini example: μ2 = 3, μ4 = 36. β2 = 36 ÷ 9 = 4 > 3, so leptokurtic; γ2 = 1.

concepts.title: Normal curve values to remember
concepts.body:
• Normal distribution: μ3 = 0, β1 = 0, γ1 = 0, β2 = 3, γ2 = 0.
  • All odd central moments of a symmetric distribution are 0.
  • For a normal curve, μ4 = 3σ⁴.

varieties.name: Raw and central moments
varieties.how: Mean = A + μ′₁. Then μ₂ = μ′₂ − μ′₁², μ₃ = μ′₃ − 3μ′₂μ′₁ + 2μ′₁³.

example.q: The first three moments about 4 are 1, 10 and 30. Find the mean, the variance and μ₃.

varieties.name: Karl Pearson's skewness
varieties.how: Use (Mean − Mode) ÷ σ, or 3(Mean − Median) ÷ σ when the mode is not given.

example.q: Mean = 45, median = 42 and SD = 9. Find Karl Pearson's coefficient of skewness.
steps: Mode is not given, so use the median form.

varieties.name: Bowley's quartile skewness
varieties.how: Sk = (Q₃ + Q₁ − 2 Median) ÷ (Q₃ − Q₁). Kelly uses P₉₀, P₅₀, P₁₀ the same way.

example.q: Q₁ = 25, median = 32 and Q₃ = 45. Find Bowley's coefficient of skewness.

varieties.name: Moment skewness β₁ and γ₁
varieties.how: β₁ = μ₃² ÷ μ₂³. γ₁ = μ₃ ÷ σ³; its sign is the sign of μ₃.

example.q: μ₂ = 4 and μ₃ = 4. Find β₁ and γ₁.
steps: μ₃ is positive, so the distribution is positively skewed.

varieties.name: Kurtosis β₂ and γ₂
varieties.how: β₂ = μ₄ ÷ μ₂². Compare with 3: above 3 lepto, equal meso, below platy.

example.q: μ₂ = 3 and μ₄ = 36. Find β₂ and name the curve.
steps: β₂ > 3 means more peaked than normal.

varieties.name: Shape from mean, median and mode
varieties.how: Mean is pulled toward the long tail. Mean > Median > Mode is positive skew; the reverse is negative.

example.q: In a distribution, mean = 50, median = 52 and mode = 55. What kind of skewness is this?
steps: The mean is pulled to the left, so the long tail is on the left.

tips: μ₁ about the mean is always 0 and μ₂ is the variance. Mean = A + μ′₁.
Write the conversions once from the binomial pattern: μ₃ = μ′₃ − 3μ′₂μ′₁ + 2μ′₁³.
β₁ is never negative; use γ₁ or the sign of μ₃ for the direction.
β₂ = 3 is the normal curve. Lepto above 3, platy below 3.
Bowley's coefficient always lies between −1 and +1; it is zero when the quartiles are equally spaced from the median.
Positive skew: Mean > Median > Mode and Q₃ − Md > Md − Q₁.
traps: Central moments do not change with origin, but they change with scale: μᵣ(x) = hʳ μᵣ(u).
In β₂ the denominator is μ₂ squared, not μ₂; in β₁ it is μ₂ cubed.
Pearson's median form has a 3 in front: 3(Mean − Median) ÷ σ.
Skewness is not dispersion: two curves can have the same SD and opposite skewness.

questions.q: The first central moment (about the mean) of any distribution is always:
questions.solution: μ<sub>1</sub> = Σ(x − x̄)/n = 0, because positive and negative deviations from the mean cancel out.

questions.q: Mean = 60, mode = 55 and SD = 10. Karl Pearson's coefficient of skewness is:
Q<sub>1</sub> = 20, median = 30 and Q<sub>3</sub> = 50. Bowley's coefficient of skewness is:
For a distribution μ<sub>2</sub> = 4 and μ<sub>4</sub> = 48. The distribution is:
questions.solution: β<sub>2</sub> = μ<sub>4</sub>/μ<sub>2</sub>² = 48/16 = 3. β<sub>2</sub> = 3 means mesokurtic (same peakedness as the normal curve).

questions.q: The first two moments about the value 5 are 2 and 20. The standard deviation is:
questions.solution:
μ2 = μ'2 − (μ'1)² = 20 − 2² = 16.
SD = √16 = 4. (Variance does not depend on the point about which raw moments are taken.)

questions.q: For a distribution μ<sub>2</sub> = 4 and μ<sub>3</sub> = −8. Then β<sub>1</sub> and the direction of skewness are:
questions.solution:
β1 = μ3²/μ2³ = 64/64 = 1.
β1 is always positive; the sign of μ3 (negative) shows the skewness is negative. (γ1 = μ3/σ³ = −8/8 = −1.)
